misconceptions.statement: Diamond and graphite are different substances made of different elements.
misconceptions.why: They look and behave so differently that students assume they must be made of different things.
misconceptions.fix: Both are made only of carbon atoms. They differ only in how the atoms are arranged.

probe.question: What element is diamond made of, and what is graphite made of?
probe.wrong_answer: Diamond is made of a special crystal element and graphite is made of lead.

misconceptions.root_belief: different looking things must be made of different stuff
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student ideas on substances and chemical identity

misconceptions.statement: Allotropes are compounds of carbon with other elements.
misconceptions.why: The word allotrope is new and students link carbon forms with compounds like CO2.
misconceptions.fix: Allotropes are different forms of the same pure element. Diamond and graphite contain only carbon.

probe.question: Is diamond an element or a compound?
probe.wrong_answer: A compound, because it has different properties from carbon.

misconceptions.root_belief: a new technical word means something familiar

misconceptions.statement: Same atoms must give same properties, so diamond and graphite should behave alike.
misconceptions.why: Students think properties belong to the atom alone, not to how atoms are joined.
misconceptions.fix: Properties depend on how atoms are bonded and arranged. The same carbon atoms give very different materials.

probe.question: Why is diamond hard but graphite soft if both are carbon?
probe.wrong_answer: They cannot both be pure carbon, since pure carbon would have one hardness.

misconceptions.root_belief: properties come only from the type of particle
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student ideas about structure-property relationships

misconceptions.statement: Diamond is held together by weak forces, so it is hard only because it is dense.
misconceptions.why: Students link hardness to heaviness or density instead of bonding.
misconceptions.fix: Each carbon in diamond forms four strong covalent bonds in a rigid 3D network, which makes it very hard.

probe.question: Why is diamond the hardest natural substance?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it is very heavy and packed tightly.

misconceptions.root_belief: heavier or denser means stronger

misconceptions.statement: Since diamond is hardest, all carbon forms must be hard.
misconceptions.why: Students overgeneralise from the most famous allotrope.
misconceptions.fix: Graphite and charcoal are soft. Only diamond's bonding makes it extremely hard.

probe.question: Is graphite as hard as diamond since both are carbon?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, carbon is always hard.

misconceptions.root_belief: one example represents the whole group

misconceptions.statement: Diamond does not conduct because it is a non-metal, and all non-metals insulate, so graphite should too.
misconceptions.why: The rule that non-metals are insulators is overgeneralised.
misconceptions.fix: Diamond has no free electrons. Graphite is a non-metal but conducts because one electron per atom is free.

probe.question: Can any non-metal conduct electricity?
probe.wrong_answer: No, no non-metal can conduct.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one group works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on student ideas of conduction and categories of metals and non-metals

misconceptions.statement: Diamond does not conduct because it is transparent and shiny.
misconceptions.why: Students link conduction to appearance rather than electrons.
misconceptions.fix: Diamond does not conduct because all four outer electrons of each atom are used in bonds, leaving none free to move.

probe.question: Why does diamond not conduct electricity?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it is clear and glassy.

misconceptions.root_belief: appearance decides the behaviour of a substance

misconceptions.statement: In graphite each carbon atom is bonded to four others, just like diamond.
misconceptions.why: Students remember carbon's valency of four and apply it to every form.
misconceptions.fix: In graphite each carbon bonds to three others in flat hexagonal layers, leaving one electron free.

probe.question: How many carbon atoms is each carbon joined to in graphite?
probe.wrong_answer: Four.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case applies to all

misconceptions.statement: Graphite conducts because it contains metal, such as lead.
misconceptions.why: Conduction is strongly associated with metals and the name pencil lead.
misconceptions.fix: Graphite is pure carbon. It conducts because of one free electron per carbon atom that can move between layers.

probe.question: Why does graphite conduct electricity?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it has lead, a metal, inside.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on student ideas that only metals conduct

misconceptions.statement: Electricity flows through graphite because the carbon atoms themselves travel along.
misconceptions.why: Students picture current as matter moving rather than charge carriers.
misconceptions.fix: The atoms stay in place. Only free electrons move through graphite to carry the current.

probe.question: What moves in graphite when current flows?
probe.wrong_answer: The carbon atoms.

misconceptions.root_belief: current is a material that flows
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student models of electric current

misconceptions.statement: Graphite is soft because its carbon atoms are weak and break easily.
misconceptions.why: Students think softness means weak atoms rather than weak forces between layers.
misconceptions.fix: Bonds inside layers are strong. Layers are held weakly together so they slide over each other.

probe.question: Why is graphite soft and slippery?
probe.wrong_answer: Its atoms are weaker than diamond atoms.

misconceptions.root_belief: whole properties are properties of single particles
misconceptions.source_hint: research on particle-level explanations of macroscopic properties

misconceptions.statement: Pencil lead is made of the metal lead.
misconceptions.why: The everyday name pencil lead matches the metal's name.
misconceptions.fix: The writing core is graphite mixed with clay. It leaves marks because layers rub off. Lead is a toxic metal not used in pencils.

probe.question: What is the black core of a pencil made of?
probe.wrong_answer: The metal lead.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: common documented misconception in science education literature

misconceptions.statement: Fullerene is a huge crystal like diamond with endless atoms.
misconceptions.why: Students assume every carbon allotrope is a giant network.
misconceptions.fix: Fullerene such as C-60 is a small hollow molecule of 60 carbon atoms shaped like a football.

probe.question: What is the structure of C-60 fullerene?
probe.wrong_answer: A giant network of carbon atoms like diamond.

misconceptions.root_belief: all members of a group share one structure

misconceptions.statement: Fullerene is a compound because it has a formula with a number like C-60.
misconceptions.why: Students think any formula with a subscript means a compound.
misconceptions.fix: C-60 contains only carbon atoms, so it is an element in molecular form, like O2 or S8.

probe.question: Is C-60 an element or compound?
probe.wrong_answer: A compound, as it has a formula.

misconceptions.root_belief: a formula with numbers means a compound

misconceptions.statement: Charcoal is made by burning wood completely in plenty of air.
misconceptions.why: Students equate making charcoal with ordinary burning.
misconceptions.fix: Charcoal forms when wood is heated strongly with very little air, so it does not burn completely.

probe.question: How is charcoal made from wood?
probe.wrong_answer: By burning wood fully until only ash is left.

misconceptions.root_belief: heating always means burning

misconceptions.statement: Charcoal, coke and soot are pure carbon, all of the same purity as diamond.
misconceptions.why: They are all called carbon forms, so students assume they are pure.
misconceptions.fix: These amorphous forms are impure and have tiny irregular carbon particles, often with other materials like tar or ash.

probe.question: Is soot as pure as a diamond?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, both are pure carbon.

misconceptions.root_belief: same name means same purity or form

misconceptions.statement: Coke is the same thing as coal.
misconceptions.why: Both are black, solid fuels so students treat them as one.
misconceptions.fix: Coke is made by heating coal without air, which removes volatile matter, leaving mostly carbon.

probe.question: What is the difference between coal and coke?
probe.wrong_answer: No difference, they are the same.

misconceptions.root_belief: things that look alike are the same thing

misconceptions.statement: Soot is a kind of dust or dirt from the air that settles on the flame.
misconceptions.why: Students see soot as something that was already present, not newly formed.
misconceptions.fix: Soot is unburnt carbon made when a fuel burns with too little oxygen.

probe.question: Why does a candle flame with low air supply give black soot?
probe.wrong_answer: Dust from the air sticks to the flame.

misconceptions.root_belief: products were already present before the change
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student ideas about combustion and conservation of matter

misconceptions.statement: When carbon burns, it disappears because it turns into nothing.
misconceptions.why: Gaseous products are invisible, so students think matter vanishes.
misconceptions.fix: Carbon joins with oxygen to form carbon dioxide gas, so the carbon is conserved in the gas.

probe.question: When charcoal burns and leaves little ash, where does the carbon go?
probe.wrong_answer: It is destroyed.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student ideas about combustion and disappearing mass

misconceptions.statement: Carbon dioxide is a poisonous gas that kills people when breathed.
misconceptions.why: Students mix it up with carbon monoxide and with its link to pollution.
misconceptions.fix: CO2 is not toxic. It is exhaled and used by plants. Very high levels only displace oxygen.

probe.question: Is CO2 a poison like CO?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is a poisonous gas.

misconceptions.root_belief: similar names mean similar properties
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student ideas about carbon dioxide and pollution

misconceptions.statement: CO2 burns well because it contains carbon and oxygen.
misconceptions.why: Students think anything with carbon is a fuel.
misconceptions.fix: CO2 is the fully burnt product so it cannot burn and puts out flames.

probe.question: Can CO2 be burnt as fuel?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it contains carbon.

misconceptions.root_belief: containing a fuel element makes it a fuel

misconceptions.statement: Carbon monoxide forms when there is plenty of oxygen.
misconceptions.why: Students think more burning means more harmful product.
misconceptions.fix: Plenty of oxygen gives CO2. CO forms when oxygen is limited and burning is incomplete.

probe.question: A coal stove in a closed room makes which gas?
probe.wrong_answer: CO2, because the room is closed.

misconceptions.root_belief: one product always forms from a given fuel

misconceptions.statement: Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it burns the lungs.
misconceptions.why: Students expect poisons to damage tissue visibly.
misconceptions.fix: CO binds to haemoglobin in blood much better than oxygen, so the body cannot carry oxygen.

probe.question: How does CO harm the body?
probe.wrong_answer: It burns the lungs.

misconceptions.root_belief: harm needs visible damage

misconceptions.statement: A gas you cannot smell or see is harmless.
misconceptions.why: Students rely on senses to judge danger.
misconceptions.fix: CO is colourless and odourless but deadly, so it needs detectors and ventilation.

probe.question: A heater room has no smell. Is it safe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, no smell means no danger.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot sense is not dangerous
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student ideas about invisible gases
